No. 

The story relies almost entirely on exteriority—focusing heavily on the physical setting (the fog, the river), the mechanical actions of operating the ferry, and brief, surface-level observations of the passengers. There is very little interiority; the reader is rarely privy to Ilse's deeper thoughts, memories, or feelings. Because her internal life is kept so distant, the narrative lacks emotional flexibility and does not portray a broad spectrum of emotions. Even at the end, when a moment of potential emotional conflict arises (the phone call from Jonas), it is handled purely through external action (looking at the deck and pressing the button to silence the phone) without any introspection or insight into how she feels about it.
